title: The Three-Phase Synchronous Motor: V-Curves, Power Factor Control & Load Dynamics

content.aim: To study operating characteristics of three-phase synchronous motor on no-load and on-load, examine effect of DC field excitation on armature current and power factor (V-curves and inverted V-curves), understand constant-speed operation and determine pull-out torque and stability limits.
objectives: To investigate operation on no-load (radial flux, zero net torque) and on-load (angular displacement load angle δ and torque generation).
To understand constant-speed operation Ns=120f/P (1500rpm for 4-pole 50Hz) independent of load up to pull-out limit.
To measure armature current Ia and power factor cosφ as field current If varied across under-excited, normally excited and over-excited regions and plot V-curves and inverted V-curves.
To load motor using coupled DC dynamometer generator and measure electrical input power, output torque and efficiency.
To determine pull-out torque and observe loss of synchronism when maximum torque exceeded.

theory.text:
Structure and Synchronous Speed

Synchronous motor has two main parts:

• Stator (Armature): Contains balanced three-phase distributed winding. When fed three-phase AC of frequency f, it produces rotating magnetic field (RMF) rotating at synchronous speed:

ns = f/p rev/s = 120f/P rev/min

where P is total poles, p=P/2 pole pairs. For 4-pole 50Hz machine: Ns=120*50/4=1500rpm, ωs=157.08 rad/s.

• Rotor (Field): Carries DC-excited field windings via slip rings, establishing alternate North-South poles fixed to rotor.

Magnetic Locking and Starting

For continuous unidirectional torque, rotor field must lock with stator RMF at same speed and direction. If rotor stationary, RMF sweeps across rotor poles at 1500rpm, force alternates clockwise and counter-clockwise every half-cycle (10ms at 50Hz). Due to rotor inertia, average torque over cycle is zero:

Tavg=0

Hence synchronous motor has zero starting torque and cannot self-start. It must be brought near synchronous speed (>95% Ns) by damper (amortisseur) bars embedded in pole faces acting as induction motor, then DC field applied to pull into synchronism.

No-Load vs On-Load Operation

• No-load: Magnetic lines cross air gap radially. Stator and rotor pole axes coincide, no tangential force, torque only enough to overcome friction and windage.

• On-load: When shaft torque applied, rotor retards by load angle δ (torque angle) relative to stator field. Magnetic lines stretch tangentially, developing restoring torque:

T = 3V Ef/(ωs Xs) sinδ

where V is stator phase voltage, Ef is excitation back-EMF, Xs is synchronous reactance.

• Pull-out: As load increases, δ increases, torque increases. Maximum at δ=90°:

Tmax=Tpull-out=3V Ef/(ωs Xs)

If load exceeds Tmax, rotor loses synchronism, stalls with large current surge.

Equivalent Circuit and Phasor

Per-phase equivalent: V = Ef + Ia Zs = Ef + Ia(Ra + jXs), where Xs = Xl + Xa (leakage + armature reaction). Since Ra<<Xs:

Ia = (V - Ef)/(jXs) = Er/(jXs) where Er=V-Ef is resultant voltage driving armature current.

V-Curves and Power Factor Control

Varying If controls Ef (Ef ∝ Φrotor ∝ If). For fixed shaft power P=3V Ia cosφ=const, active component Ia cosφ remains constant, so reactive component changes:

• Normal excitation (Ef cosδ=V): Motor draws only active current, Ia minimum, unity PF (cosφ=1.00).

• Under-excitation (Ef<V): Rotor flux insufficient, motor draws lagging reactive current from mains for magnetizing, lagging PF.

• Over-excitation (Ef>V): Rotor flux excessive, motor supplies reactive power to grid, draws leading current, acts as capacitor.

Plotting Ia vs If gives V-curves, plotting cosφ vs If gives inverted V-curves. Over-excited uncoupled synchronous motor running on no-load to supply leading VARs is called synchronous condenser, used for power factor correction and voltage control in transmission systems.

Torque Angle Stability and Hunting

Load angle δ is angular displacement between rotor and stator fields. Stable region is 0<δ<90° where dT/dδ>0. Beyond 90°, dT/dδ<0 and system unstable. Pull-out torque can be increased by increasing Ef or reducing Xs.

Hunting is oscillation of rotor about steady-state δ due to sudden load or voltage changes, caused by inertia. Frequency determined by synchronizing torque and inertia. If hunting frequency matches natural frequency of supply, resonance can cause loss of synchronism. Damper windings provide induction torque opposing relative motion, damping oscillations. Damper bars are copper/bronze bars embedded in pole shoes short-circuited by end rings, acting as squirrel-cage winding. During synchronous operation at Ns, no relative motion, no induced current. During hunting, relative motion induces currents producing damping torque.

Additional Analysis: V-Curves Derivation and Synchronous Condenser Application

V-curves show armature current Ia versus field current If for constant mechanical load. For fixed output power Pout = 3V Ia cosφ = constant (neglecting losses, Pin≈Pout), active component Ia cosφ = P/(3V) = constant. As If varies, Ef = 4.44 f N Φ ∝ If changes, changing reactive power. At low If (under-excitation), Ef small, motor needs lagging reactive current from supply to provide magnetizing flux, so Ia large lagging, cosφ lagging low. As If increases, Ef increases, lagging reactive demand decreases, Ia decreases to minimum at unity PF where Ef cosδ≈V and all current is active. Further increase in If (over-excitation) makes Ef>V, motor supplies leading reactive power to grid, Ia increases again leading, cosφ leading. Hence Ia vs If is V-shaped with minimum at unity PF.

Inverted V-curves show PF vs If, peaking at unity at normal excitation, falling to low lagging at low If and low leading at high If. For no-load, active power is small (only friction and windage), so Ia cosφ small, V-curve minimum current small (0.58A). Under load, active power larger, so minimum Ia larger (1.92A at 2A generator load).

Synchronous condenser is synchronous motor running without mechanical load, over-excited to supply leading VARs for PF correction and voltage control. Unlike capacitor banks switched in discrete steps, synchronous condenser can continuously vary reactive output by varying field current, and can both supply and absorb VARs (over-excited leading, under-excited lagging). It also provides inertia and short-circuit strength, valuable in systems with high renewable penetration where synchronous inertia is low. In Nigeria, TCN uses synchronous condensers in some transmission substations for voltage control. Disadvantages include higher losses than capacitors (friction, windage, field copper loss), need for maintenance (bearings, brushes, slip rings) and higher capital cost. Modern alternatives include SVC (Static VAR Compensator) using thyristor-switched capacitors/reactors and STATCOM using voltage-source converter, offering faster response and lower maintenance.

Stability and Pull-Out Torque

Electromagnetic torque T = 3V Ef/(ωs Xs) sinδ, where δ is load angle between V and Ef phasors. At no-load δ≈0, small torque to overcome losses. As mechanical load increases, rotor retards, δ increases, sinδ increases, torque increases to balance load. Maximum torque at δ=90°, Tmax=3V Ef/(ωs Xs). If load torque exceeds Tmax, rotor cannot develop enough torque, δ increases beyond 90°, sinδ decreases, torque decreases while load torque remains, causing rotor to decelerate rapidly and lose synchronism, stalling with large current surge (5-8 times rated) as machine acts as induction motor with slip=1 but without proper rotor circuit. In experiment, pull-out occurred at generator current 4.8A, corresponding to mechanical output 1056W, torque 6.72 N·m, δ≈88°, close to theoretical 90° limit.

Hunting and Damping

Hunting is oscillation of rotor about steady-state δ due to sudden disturbances (load change, voltage dip, fault). Rotor inertia causes overshoot beyond new equilibrium δ, then oscillation at natural frequency determined by synchronizing torque coefficient (dT/dδ) and inertia J. If hunting frequency matches supply or mechanical natural frequency, resonance can cause δ to exceed 90° and loss of synchronism. Damper (amortisseur) windings are copper/bronze bars embedded in pole shoes, short-circuited by end rings, forming squirrel-cage winding. During synchronous operation at Ns, no relative motion between damper bars and RMF, no induced EMF/current. During hunting, rotor speed oscillates above/below Ns, relative motion induces currents in damper bars by Faraday's law, producing induction torque opposing relative motion (Lenz's law), damping oscillations. Damper windings also provide starting torque as induction motor, allowing synchronous motor to start as induction motor and pull into synchronism when field applied near synchronous speed, as demonstrated in lab.

procedure: BKB universal machine set wired as per Figure 306.1a: 3-phase stator winding connected to 3-phase Variac through main switch S1. Ammeter A1 in series with Phase A, two wattmeters W1,W2 and voltmeter V across lines. Rotor field winding connected to 220V DC supply via field switch S2, ammeter A2 and rheostat R1. Wiring checked by supervisor.
Field rheostat R1 set to maximum resistance and Variac dial to zero. Rotor shaft checked for free rotation.

Starting: Switch S1 closed, Variac gradually increased until voltmeter read 220V AC. Motor accelerated as induction motor via damper winding. When speed neared 1450rpm, DC field switch S2 closed. Rotor pulled into synchronism at exactly 1500rpm.

No-load V-curves: Field rheostat adjusted to obtain If=0.50A, meters A1,A2,W1,W2,V recorded. If increased in steps of 0.3-0.4A up to 3.00A, all instruments recorded into Table 306.1. At low PF (<0.5), W1 deflected negative and recorded as negative as per two-wattmeter method.
Normal excitation point where A1 minimum (0.58A) and W1=W2 (unity PF) identified at If≈1.85A no-load.
DC dynamometer generator coupled to load resistor bank as per Figure 306.1b for loading tests.

Constant load / variable excitation: Motor brought to synchronous speed, generator adjusted to deliver Igen=2.0A at 220V DC. Motor field If varied from 1.0A to 3.0A, instruments logged into Table 306.2. Speed remained 1500rpm throughout, confirming constant-speed characteristic.

Variable load / constant excitation: Motor field set to optimal normal excitation If=1.95A and held constant. Generator load current increased in steps of 1.0A up to 4.0A, armature current, input power and speed recorded. Torque T=Pout/ωs and efficiency calculated as in Table 306.3.
Pull-out test: Load increased beyond 4.5A. At about 4.8A generator current, loss of synchronism occurred with vibration and current surge >12A. Main switch S1 opened immediately to protect machine.
precautions: DC field switch S2 not opened abruptly while field current flowed. Highly inductive rotor winding can generate spike L di/dt >2000V that can damage insulation and cause shock. Field current reduced to minimum via rheostat before switching OFF.

In two-wattmeter method at low PF (cosφ<0.5), wattmeter W1 deflects backward (negative). Current coil connections not reversed; instead voltage coil reversed and reading recorded as negative (P=W2-W1).
On loss of synchronism during overload test, main AC stator switch S1 tripped immediately. Stalled machine draws 5-8 times rated blocked-rotor current and can burn stator winding within seconds.
content.discussion:
V-Curves (Graph 306.1) showed V-shaped trajectory of armature current Ia versus field current If. At low excitation If=0.50A, Ia=3.80A lagging with cosφ=0.138 lag. As excitation increased, rotor supplied more of its own magnetizing flux, reactive demand from stator decreased and Ia fell to minimum 0.58A at If=1.85A where PF≈1.00. Beyond this, over-excitation caused stator to deliver leading reactive current, Ia rose to 3.15A at If=3.00A with cosφ=0.204 leading. This V-shape occurs because for fixed mechanical power P=3V Ia cosφ=const, active component Ia cosφ must remain constant, so as PF changes, Ia first decreases to minimum at unity PF then increases.

Under mechanical load (Tables 306.2 and 306.3), motor maintained constant speed 1500rpm from no-load to full load. Unlike induction motor that requires slip to develop torque, synchronous motor remains magnetically locked to 50Hz RMF. As load increased, rotor retarded by load angle δ, shifting Ef phasor backward and producing tangential magnetic force to balance shaft torque. Load angle δ increased from about 2° at no-load to 55° at 4.0A load, approaching 88° at pull-out.

During overload pull-out test, when generator load reached 5.0A, load torque exceeded maximum pull-out torque Tmax=6.72 N·m at δ≈90°. Beyond δ=90°, torque decreases because d/dδ(sinδ)<0, causing instability. Magnetic coupling broke, rotor stalled and current surged over 12A, requiring immediate tripping of S1. This confirms stability limit at δ=90°.

Two-wattmeter method showed expected behaviour: at low PF (<0.5) W1 negative, at unity PF W1=W2, at leading PF W2 negative. This matches W1=VL IL cos(30+φ), W2=VL IL cos(30-φ). At unity PF, φ=0, W1=W2=VL IL cos30.

The ability to operate at leading PF by over-excitation makes synchronous motor useful as synchronous condenser for power factor correction and voltage control. Over-excited synchronous motor draws leading current, acting as capacitor supplying leading VARs to grid. This can be continuously varied by field current, unlike capacitor banks switched in steps. In transmission systems, synchronous condensers provide smooth VAR control, inertia and short-circuit strength.

Hunting phenomenon was discussed: sudden load or voltage changes cause rotor to oscillate about steady-state δ due to inertia. Damper windings (amortisseur) consisting of copper bars embedded in pole shoes short-circuited by end rings act as squirrel-cage winding. During synchronous operation no induced current, but during hunting relative motion induces currents producing damping torque proportional to slip, quenching oscillations. Damper windings also provide starting torque as induction motor.

Overall, constant-speed characteristic, V-curves and pull-out limit were verified experimentally.

content.conclusion: Experiment verified synchronous motor characteristics. Starting via damper winding as induction motor and pulling into synchronism at 1500rpm when DC field applied was demonstrated. V-curves and inverted V-curves confirmed field excitation controls armature current and power factor: lagging under under-excitation, unity at normal excitation (If≈1.85A no-load, 1.95A on-load), leading under over-excitation, confirming operation as synchronous condenser. Under varying load with constant excitation, speed remained constant at 1500rpm. Pull-out torque determined as 6.72 N·m at 4.8A generator current, verifying stability limit at δ=90°. Two-wattmeter behaviour at low PF and damping role of amortisseur windings were also observed.

questions.question: Calculate the mechanical shaft torque developed by the synchronous motor in each loading case recorded in Table 306.3.
questions.answer: T = Pmech/ωs, ωs=2πNs/60=2π*1500/60=157.08 rad/s. At Igen=1.0A Pout=220W T=1.40 N·m, 2.0A 440W T=2.80 N·m, 3.0A 660W T=4.20 N·m, 4.0A 880W T=5.60 N·m, pull-out 1056W T=6.72 N·m, as listed in Table 306.3.

questions.question: Determine the most favorable field excitation current from your graph of armature current versus field current. Explain why this excitation is optimal.
questions.answer: From V-curve, most favorable If=1.85A no-load (1.95A on-load). At this point motor operates at unity PF (cosφ=1.00) and armature current minimum (0.58A no-load), minimizing I²Ra copper losses and maximizing efficiency. Unity PF eliminates reactive kVA burden on supply and avoids voltage regulation issues and utility penalties. In industry, operating at unity or slightly leading PF is preferred.

questions.question: What are the necessary physical and electrical conditions required for a synchronous motor to reach synchronous speed?
questions.answer:
• Auxiliary acceleration to near-synchronous speed (>95% Ns, >1425rpm for 1500rpm machine) by damper windings or auxiliary motor, since starting torque zero.
• DC field applied only when slip small enough for poles to pull into step within half slip cycle (closed near 1450rpm in experiment).
• Balanced three-phase AC supply with correct phase sequence A-B-C and stable frequency to produce smooth constant-velocity RMF.

questions.question: Did the motor fail (lose synchronism) in your experiment when the mechanical load was increased? If so, explain the exact electromagnetic mechanism causing the failure.
questions.answer: Yes, motor lost synchronism beyond Igen=4.8A. Torque T=3V Ef/(ωs Xs) sinδ. As load increases, δ increases. Maximum at δ=90°. When shaft load exceeds pull-out torque, required torque cannot be developed. Beyond 90°, developed torque decreases (d/dδ sinδ<0), rotor decelerates rapidly, magnetic interlock shears, motor falls out of step, vibrates and draws large short-circuit currents until de-energized. Observed as vibration, speed drop and current surge >12A, requiring immediate trip of S1.

questions.question: Explain the phenomenon of "Hunting" (Phase Swinging) in synchronous motors, and describe how Damper (Amortisseur) Windings suppress it.
questions.answer:
When synchronous motor experiences sudden disturbance (load change, voltage dip), rotor cannot instantly settle at new equilibrium δ. Due to inertia, it overshoots new δ, oscillates mechanically about steady-state angle. This periodic oscillation around synchronous speed is hunting. If hunting frequency matches natural frequency of supply system, resonance can cause δ>90° and loss of synchronism.
Damper windings are copper/bronze bars embedded in pole shoes short-circuited by end rings (like squirrel-cage). At steady synchronous speed, no relative motion, no induced current. During hunting, rotor oscillates above/below Ns, creating relative velocity between damper bars and stator field, inducing circulating currents by Faraday's and Lenz's laws. These currents produce damping torque opposing relative motion, quenching oscillation and restoring smooth operation. Damper bars also provide starting torque.

learnings: Visualization of magnetic locking between rotor poles and stator RMF and concept of torque angle δ and how it increases with load to develop torque.
Power factor control: synchronous motor can operate at lagging, unity and leading PF by adjusting DC field current, acting as synchronous condenser for PF correction.
Verification of absolute speed constancy at 1500rpm irrespective of load up to pull-out, unlike induction motor that requires slip.
Safety handling of highly inductive DC field circuits, interpretation of negative wattmeter readings in two-wattmeter method and rapid response to loss of synchronism, important for plant operation.
